note: Dropped the "since even as it was" and "although" connectives that carry the logic.
replacement: About the same time in the summer, Brasidas set out on his march to the Thracian places with seventeen hundred heavy infantry. Arriving at Heraclea in Trachis, he sent a messenger from there to his friends at Pharsalus, asking them to conduct him and his army through the country. So there came to Melitia in Achaia Panaerus, Dorus, Hippolochidas, Torylaus and Strophacus, the Chalcidian proxenus, and under their escort he resumed his march. Other Thessalians accompanied him as well, among them Niconidas from Larissa, a friend of Perdiccas. It was never very easy to cross Thessaly without an escort, and throughout Hellas it was a delicate step for an armed force to pass without leave through a neighbor’s country. Besides this, the Thessalian people had always sympathized with the Athenians. Indeed, if Thessaly had had a constitutional government instead of its customary close oligarchy, he would never have been able to go on, since even as it was he was met at the river Enipeus by certain men of the opposite party, who forbade him to go further and complained that he was making the attempt without the consent of the nation. His escort answered that they had no intention of taking him through against their will; they were only friends attending an unexpected visitor. Brasidas himself added that he came as a friend to Thessaly and its inhabitants, that his arms were directed not against them but against the Athenians, with whom he was at war, and that although he knew of no quarrel between the Thessalians and the Lacedaemonians to prevent the two nations from having access to each other’s territory, he neither would nor could go on against their wishes; he could only beg them not to stop him. With this answer they went away. He then took the advice of his escort and pushed on without halting, before a greater force could gather to prevent him. So on the very day he set out from Melitia he covered the whole distance to Pharsalus and encamped on the river Apidanus. From there he went on to Phacium, and from Phacium to Perrhaebia. Here his Thessalian escort turned back, and the Perrhaebians, who are subjects of Thessaly, set him down at Dium in the dominions of Perdiccas. Dium is a Macedonian town under Mount Olympus, facing Thessaly.

note: "None of them need be calmer than they should be" garbles the source meaning that none need be more at ease than they.
replacement: “Some of you may hold back because they have private enemies, and fear that I will hand the city over to a party. None need be more at ease than they. I have not come to help this party or that. I would not call it bringing you freedom in any real sense if I ignored your constitution and enslaved the many to the few or the few to the many. That would be heavier than a foreign yoke, and we Lacedaemonians, instead of earning thanks for our trouble, would win neither honor nor glory, but reproaches instead. The very charges that strengthen our hands in the war against the Athenians would, by our own admission, apply to us, and be more hateful in us than in those who make no claim to honesty. For it is more disgraceful for men of character to seize what they covet by plausible fraud than by open force. Force has at least the justification of the might that fortune gives; the other is plain roguery, however clever. A matter that touches us so closely we naturally guard most jealously. And beyond the oaths I have mentioned, what stronger assurance can you have than this: that when you set our words beside the facts, you are convinced it is in our interest to do as we say?

note: "The other Boeotarchs, eleven in all" misstates "the rest of the eleven Boeotarchs" (Pagondas was one of the eleven).
replacement: While the Athenians were thus occupied, the Boeotians were mustering at Tanagra. By the time they had come in from all the towns, the Athenians were already on their way home. The rest of the eleven Boeotarchs were against giving battle, because the enemy was no longer in Boeotia; the Athenians had halted just across the Oropian border.
